# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees work across functions, locations, and systems that generate and consume substantial amounts of information every day. Employees spend considerable time searching for policies, procedures, project documentation, expertise, and operational guidance. This creates avoidable delays, inconsistent answers, duplicated work, and an ongoing burden on subject-matter experts.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, organization-specific assistant that can answer questions, summarize documents, draft content, support analysis, and help employees navigate internal processes. A properly governed internal AI assistant can improve productivity while preserving existing approval structures, data protections, and accountability.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The assistant will be designed as a secure, centrally governed service that uses approved internal information sources and integrates with existing collaboration, identity, and business platforms. Deployment will begin with carefully selected use cases and user groups, followed by measured expansion based on performance, employee feedback, risk assessment, and demonstrated business value.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, accessible, and secure AI assistant that reduces the time required to find information, complete routine knowledge work, and access organizational expertise.

The project will pursue the following outcomes:

- Improve employee productivity by reducing time spent searching for information, drafting routine materials, summarizing content, and navigating internal processes.
- Provide consistent access to approved policies, procedures, standards, and organizational knowledge.
- Enable employees to use AI within approved security, privacy, legal, and records-management controls.
- Establish a repeatable governance model for AI use, including human oversight, data classification, monitoring, incident response, and acceptable-use standards.
- Identify and scale high-value use cases across corporate, operational, customer-facing, and support functions.
- Develop employee capability and confidence through training, communications, and practical guidance.
- Create a foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and integrations without prematurely automating high-risk decisions.

Success will be measured not only by adoption, but also by the quality of answers, reduction in time spent on target tasks, user trust, risk management performance, and measurable value to business functions.

## Scope

The project will deliver an enterprise internal AI assistant accessible through approved organizational channels, such as the company intranet, collaboration platform, or employee portal. Access will be controlled through the organization’s identity and access-management systems, with permissions aligned to employees’ existing roles and source-system entitlements.

The initial assistant will support common, lower-risk activities including answering questions about approved internal information, summarizing documents, drafting emails and reports, converting notes into structured outputs, comparing policies or procedures, generating meeting preparation materials, and assisting with research across authorized sources. The assistant will clearly distinguish generated responses from authoritative source material and provide citations or links wherever feasible.

The solution will connect initially to a curated set of high-value information sources. These may include corporate policies, human-resources guidance, information-technology support content, finance and procurement procedures, compliance materials, approved process documentation, and selected knowledge repositories. Each source will be assessed for ownership, accuracy, sensitivity, access permissions, retention requirements, and readiness for AI use.

The first release will not autonomously make employment, legal, financial, safety, medical, credit, disciplinary, or other high-impact decisions. It will not replace required professional judgment, formal approvals, or established business controls. Any future expansion into workflow automation or decision support will require separate risk assessment, testing, approval, and monitoring.

The project includes platform selection or configuration, security and privacy assessment, data-source preparation, identity integration, user experience design, prompt and response safeguards, governance policies, pilot deployment, employee training, communications, support processes, and post-launch measurement.

The project excludes broad replacement of existing knowledge-management systems, unrestricted access to confidential data, autonomous execution of consequential transactions, and deployment of unapproved third-party AI tools. It also excludes the assumption that AI-generated content is accurate without human review.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will follow a phased approach over approximately twelve months, with continued optimization after enterprise launch.

During months one and two, the project team will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint business and technical owners, define governance, identify priority use cases, assess regulatory and privacy requirements, establish baseline productivity measures, and select the initial technology approach. The team will also conduct an inventory of potential information sources and classify them according to sensitivity, quality, ownership, and readiness.

During months three and four, the organization will design and configure the solution. This work will include identity and access integration, security architecture, data-ingestion patterns, source-system connectors, logging and monitoring, user-interface design, escalation processes, and initial content preparation. The team will develop acceptable-use guidance, evaluation standards, incident-management procedures, and a training plan. A representative test environment will be established using approved content.

During months five and six, the assistant will undergo technical, security, privacy, legal, and user-acceptance testing. Testing will evaluate answer quality, citation behavior, hallucination rates, prompt-injection resistance, access-control enforcement, data leakage risks, response performance, accessibility, and resilience. A controlled pilot of approximately 250 to 400 employees from selected functions will then begin. Pilot participants will receive training and structured mechanisms for reporting errors, missing content, harmful outputs, and useful applications.

During months seven and eight, the project team will analyze pilot results and make required improvements. Information sources will be expanded or restricted based on quality and risk findings. User guidance, prompts, retrieval settings, support procedures, and monitoring thresholds will be refined. The organization will confirm launch readiness through a formal review involving technology, security, privacy, legal, records management, communications, and participating business leaders.

During months nine and ten, the assistant will be deployed to a broader group of approximately 1,500 employees across representative business functions. The rollout will use a train-the-trainer model, targeted communications, office hours, demonstrations, and role-specific examples. Adoption, performance, and support data will be reviewed weekly during this phase.

During months eleven and twelve, the service will be made available to the remaining employees, subject to readiness and risk controls. Enterprise launch will include a clear acceptable-use policy, mandatory introductory training, self-service resources, support channels, and ongoing reporting to executive sponsors. After launch, the program will move into a continuous-improvement operating model, with quarterly reviews of value, risk, source quality, usage patterns, and potential new capabilities.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior leader with authority across business, technology, and risk functions. A steering committee should include representatives from information technology, information security, privacy, legal, compliance, human resources, records management, communications, accessibility, and major business units.

A core delivery team of approximately 15 to 22 full-time-equivalent personnel will be required during design, pilot, and rollout. This team should include a program director; product manager; enterprise architect; AI or machine-learning engineer; data and integration engineers; security architect; privacy and legal specialists; information and records-management representatives; user-experience and accessibility specialists; change-management and communications leads; training developers; business analysts; quality-assurance and evaluation specialists; and service-management personnel. Business units should provide part-time subject-matter experts and content owners to validate use cases, prepare source material, and review answer quality.

The technical environment will require an approved enterprise AI platform or model provider, secure application hosting, identity and access management, encryption, network controls, content connectors, document indexing or retrieval services, monitoring and logging, analytics, and service-desk integration. The architecture should support model substitution or enhancement over time to reduce vendor lock-in and accommodate changing security, cost, and performance requirements.

The organization should establish a first-year budget covering platform licensing or consumption, implementation services, integration and data preparation, security and privacy assessments, testing, training, communications, support, and contingency. A preliminary planning estimate is $2 million to $4 million for the first year, depending on technology choice, integration complexity, licensing structure, and the number of internal systems included. Ongoing annual operating costs should be assessed during the pilot and based on actual usage, support demand, model consumption, data-source maintenance, and governance requirements.

Each connected information source must have a named business owner responsible for accuracy, freshness, access permissions, and retirement of obsolete content. The program will also require a formal change-control process for adding new data sources, enabling new capabilities, modifying retention or logging settings, and expanding into higher-risk use cases.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The internal AI assistant will operate under a documented governance framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define permitted and prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, human-review obligations, accountability for generated content, retention and audit rules, accessibility expectations, and procedures for reporting and investigating incidents.

The assistant will enforce existing user permissions rather than creating a separate entitlement model. Users will receive only information they are already authorized to access, subject to validation through testing and continuous monitoring. Sensitive information will be excluded or handled through additional controls where appropriate. Prompts and responses will be protected in accordance with organizational security and privacy standards, and data will not be used to train external models unless explicitly approved.

The user experience will communicate that the assistant can produce inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, or misleading responses. Responses should identify their supporting sources where possible, and employees will be instructed to verify important information and retain responsibility for decisions and deliverables. High-impact use cases will require human review and may be restricted to approved roles.

The program will maintain evaluation datasets representing common employee questions, sensitive scenarios, adversarial prompts, and known failure modes. Performance will be monitored for accuracy, relevance, citation quality, bias, unauthorized disclosure, availability, latency, and cost. Material incidents will trigger documented containment, investigation, remediation, and communication procedures.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees through approved channels, operates within the organization’s security and privacy requirements, and has a sustainable ownership and support model.

At least 60 percent of employees should be reached through training and launch communications, with a target of 40 percent monthly active usage within six months of enterprise launch. At least 75 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete selected tasks more quickly or effectively, and at least 70 percent should express confidence that the service is appropriate for approved internal use.

For the initial priority use cases, the program should demonstrate a measurable reduction in task time, with a target of at least 20 percent for information-search, document-summarization, and routine-drafting activities. The assistant should achieve at least 85 percent acceptable-response performance on approved evaluation sets, with citations or source links available for the substantial majority of factual responses drawn from internal content.

No critical security or privacy incidents should occur as a result of unauthorized access or data exposure. All high-severity findings identified during testing must be resolved or formally accepted by the appropriate risk owner before expansion. Support demand should stabilize within three months of enterprise launch, and content owners should meet defined standards for source accuracy, freshness, and review frequency.

Finally, the program should produce a prioritized portfolio of additional use cases supported by evidence from employee feedback, usage analytics, business-value assessments, and risk reviews. Expansion will proceed only when each new capability has a named owner, a defined success measure, an appropriate control framework, and a clear human-accountability model.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization is an opportunity to improve access to knowledge, reduce routine administrative effort, and establish a responsible foundation for broader AI adoption. A phased implementation will allow the organization to demonstrate value while protecting confidential information, preserving human accountability, and learning from real employee use.

With executive sponsorship, disciplined governance, high-quality information sources, appropriate technical investment, and sustained employee enablement, the organization can deliver a trusted AI service that improves day-to-day work for its 5,000 employees and supports future digital transformation.

From weeks seven through fourteen, the team will select or confirm the technology approach and design the target architecture. This phase will include identity integration, access-control design, data-flow mapping, security and privacy assessments, vendor due diligence, content-source prioritization, and definition of evaluation standards. Deliverables will include the solution architecture, risk assessment, governance framework, initial content inventory, and pilot implementation plan.

From weeks fifteen through twenty-four, the team will configure the assistant and prepare the initial knowledge sources. Content will be classified, deduplicated where practical, reviewed by designated owners, and connected through permission-aware integrations. The project team will implement logging, monitoring, feedback mechanisms, usage policies, escalation procedures, and technical safeguards against inappropriate data exposure and unsafe outputs. A small technical pilot of approximately 100 employees will validate system performance, access controls, response quality, and support processes.

From weeks twenty-five through thirty-six, the organization will conduct a broader business pilot involving approximately 500 employees across representative departments. Pilot participants will receive role-specific training and guidance on effective and responsible use. The team will collect quantitative and qualitative feedback, test priority use cases, evaluate answer quality and source attribution, identify failure modes, and refine the service. The pilot will include formal review by information security, privacy, legal, compliance, human resources, and relevant business owners.

From weeks thirty-seven through forty-four, the assistant will be expanded to approximately 1,500 employees, with emphasis on high-value use cases and departments that have demonstrated strong content readiness. Adoption campaigns, manager toolkits, office hours, peer champions, and targeted training will support this stage. Benefits measurement will compare results with the baseline and assess whether the solution is ready for enterprise deployment.

From weeks forty-five through fifty-two, the service will be made available to the remaining employees in controlled waves. Each wave will be supported by communications, training, service-desk readiness, content-owner engagement, and usage monitoring. At the end of the initial rollout, the steering committee will review performance, risks, adoption, and benefits realization and approve the transition to steady-state operations.

After the initial twelve-month program, the assistant will enter an ongoing optimization phase. This phase will include model and prompt improvements, additional content integrations, periodic access reviews, evaluation of emerging use cases, policy updates, user research, and continuous measurement of value and risk.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior leader responsible for coordinating business priorities, technology, risk, and organizational adoption. A steering committee should include representatives from information technology, information security, privacy, legal, compliance, human resources, communications, records management, and major business functions.

A core delivery team of approximately 15 to 25 full-time equivalent staff will be required during implementation, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and content owners. Core roles should include a program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, data and integration engineers, security architect, privacy and risk specialists, content and knowledge-management leads, user-experience and service-design specialists, change-management and communications leads, training designers, business analysts, quality and evaluation specialists, and service-desk representatives.

Each participating business function will appoint content owners and use-case champions. These individuals will validate source material, identify high-value workflows, support pilot users, and help maintain content quality. Their effort is expected to be part-time during implementation and ongoing for content governance.

The technology budget will cover the AI platform or model services, retrieval and indexing capabilities, enterprise integrations, identity and access management, security controls, logging and monitoring, data storage, evaluation tooling, support capabilities, and any required user or administrator licensing. Additional funding will be needed for content remediation, training, communications, change management, independent security and privacy assessments, and contingency capacity.

The solution should be designed with scalable infrastructure, strong data segregation, configurable retention, centralized administration, and the ability to change models or vendors without requiring a complete redesign. Contracts should address data usage, confidentiality, service levels, incident notification, audit rights, data residency where required, intellectual property, and service portability.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal responsible-AI framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define permitted and prohibited uses, information-handling requirements, human-review obligations, escalation procedures, accountability for business outputs, and consequences for misuse.

Access will be based on the organization’s existing identity and authorization controls. The assistant will not bypass source-system permissions. Sensitive information will be protected through data classification, connector restrictions, encryption, retention controls, monitoring, and regular access reviews. Prompt and response data will not be used to train external models unless explicitly approved under contractual and governance requirements.

The service will provide user-facing guidance that outputs may be incomplete, inaccurate, or unsuitable for a particular decision. Where the assistant uses internal sources, responses should identify or link to the relevant material whenever technically feasible. High-impact use cases will require documented human review and, where appropriate, approval by the responsible business owner.

A cross-functional review process will assess new integrations and action-taking capabilities. The project will maintain an incident process for suspected data exposure, harmful or discriminatory outputs, policy violations, system abuse, and material service failures. Evaluation will include accuracy, relevance, groundedness, harmful-content testing, access-control testing, prompt-injection testing, privacy testing, and resilience testing.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees through approved channels, operates within established security and privacy controls, and has demonstrated measurable value in priority use cases.

Key success measures will include:

- At least 70 percent of targeted employees activated within six months of organization-wide availability.
- At least 50 percent of activated users becoming monthly active users, subject to refinement based on pilot benchmarks.
- A minimum 20 percent reduction in reported time spent locating internal information for participating users.
- A minimum 15 percent reduction in time spent on selected routine drafting, summarization, and information-processing tasks.
- User satisfaction of at least ม75 percent among active users, measured through standardized surveys.
- At least 80 percent of evaluated answers to approved knowledge questions meeting defined standards for relevance, accuracy, and appropriate source attribution.
- No material unauthorized disclosure of restricted information attributable to the service.
- Completion of security, privacy, legal, compliance, and accessibility reviews before each deployment stage.
- Completion of required training by at least 90 percent of pilot participants and employees in designated high-risk roles.
- A documented content-ownership model covering all production knowledge sources.
- Service availability and support performance meeting agreed enterprise technology standards.
- Demonstrated positive return on investment or a credible benefits case based on measured time savings, improved service quality, reduced support demand, or other validated outcomes.

Success will be assessed through a combination of platform analytics, controlled user testing, employee surveys, business-function metrics, support data, security monitoring, and periodic executive reviews. The organization will use the results not only to determine whether the initial deployment achieved its goals, but also to decide which additional integrations and automated workflows should be pursued.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to knowledge, and modernize how employees interact with information and internal services. The opportunity must be pursued with disciplined governance, secure architecture, high-quality content, transparent communication, and measurable accountability.

This proposal recommends a phased, evidence-based implementation that balances speed with responsible adoption. By beginning with controlled pilots, establishing clear safeguards, and expanding only when performance and risk criteria are met, the organization can create a trusted AI capability that delivers near-term employee value while providing a durable foundation for future innovation.

# Project Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Executive Summary

This proposal recommends deploying a secure, enterprise-grade internal AI assistant across the organization’s 5,000 employees. The assistant will help employees find and interpret company information, draft and summarize content, support routine analysis, and streamline common business processes while maintaining appropriate privacy, security, governance, and human oversight.

The deployment will begin with a controlled pilot involving representative business units and use cases, followed by a phased enterprise rollout. The program will prioritize measurable productivity gains, responsible adoption, integration with existing systems, and safeguards against unauthorized access, inaccurate outputs, data leakage, and inappropriate use. Within twelve months, the organization should have a reliable internal AI capability available to most employees, supported by clear policies, training, monitoring, and an operating model for continuous improvement.

## Background and Rationale

Generative artificial intelligence has matured into a practical productivity technology capable of assisting with research, writing, summarization, knowledge retrieval, data interpretation, and workflow support. Employees across the organization already spend significant time searching for information, preparing routine documents, responding to internal requests, summarizing meetings, and navigating fragmented knowledge systems. These activities represent an opportunity to improve productivity and employee experience without replacing human judgment or accountability.

A centrally managed internal AI assistant can provide a safer and more effective alternative to unsanctioned consumer tools. Rather than allowing employees to use disconnected applications with uncertain data practices, the organization can establish a governed platform that applies enterprise security controls, respects existing permissions, records appropriate usage information, and provides access to approved organizational knowledge.

The proposed assistant will not be positioned as an autonomous decision-maker. It will function as a support tool that helps employees work more efficiently while requiring human review for consequential decisions, external communications, regulated activities, and outputs that may affect customers, employees, finances, legal matters, or organizational reputation.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to establish a secure, scalable, and useful internal AI assistant that improves employee productivity and access to organizational knowledge.

The program will pursue six specific objectives. First, it will provide employees with a consistent AI experience through approved web, desktop, and collaboration-platform interfaces. Second, it will enable controlled access to relevant internal content, including policies, procedures, knowledge articles, templates, and other approved sources, while preserving existing access permissions. Third, it will reduce time spent on routine work such as drafting, summarizing, information retrieval, meeting preparation, and analysis. Fourth, it will create a governance framework covering acceptable use, privacy, security, intellectual property, records management, model risk, and human oversight. Fifth, it will build employee capability through targeted training, practical guidance, and an internal community of practice. Finally, it will establish measurable performance, adoption, and risk indicators to guide ongoing investment and improvement.

## Scope

The initial scope includes the selection and configuration of an enterprise AI assistant platform; integration with approved identity, collaboration, document management, and knowledge systems; implementation of security and access controls; development of policies and standards; pilot testing; employee training; communications; support processes; and phased organization-wide deployment.

The assistant’s initial capabilities will include conversational question answering, summarization, drafting and editing, translation where appropriate, meeting and document preparation, structured information extraction, and retrieval of approved internal knowledge. Selected workflows may also include generating first drafts of reports, preparing briefing materials, producing frequently requested internal responses, and assisting service-desk or operations teams with knowledge lookup.

The program will include integration with systems such as the organization’s identity provider, collaboration suite, document repositories, intranet, knowledge bases, and approved business applications. Integrations will be implemented according to data classification, access permissions, system reliability, and business value.

The initial deployment will exclude fully autonomous actions that create financial commitments, alter personnel records, approve transactions, make employment decisions, provide unsupervised legal or medical advice, or communicate externally without human review. High-risk use cases will require separate assessment and approval. Personal data, confidential information, regulated records, and commercially sensitive content will be handled according to existing policies and applicable legal requirements.

## Proposed Solution

The organization will deploy a centrally governed AI assistant using an enterprise platform that supports single sign-on, role-based access, encryption, administrative controls, auditability, data isolation, retention management, and integration with approved organizational data sources. The selected platform should provide contractual assurances that organizational data will not be used to train public models without explicit authorization and should support regional data residency and applicable regulatory requirements.

The assistant will use retrieval-augmented access to internal knowledge where appropriate. This approach allows the system to locate relevant approved content at the time of a user’s request rather than relying solely on model memory. Responses should provide citations or links to source material whenever feasible, enabling employees to verify information and identify outdated or conflicting content.

Existing permissions will remain authoritative. The assistant must not expose information to a user who could not access the underlying source directly. Content owners will remain responsible for the accuracy, classification, and lifecycle management of their information. The AI program will complement, not replace, established records-management and knowledge-management responsibilities.

A governance structure will oversee the program. An executive sponsor will provide strategic direction and resolve cross-functional issues. A steering committee representing technology, security, privacy, legal, risk, human resources, communications, and key business functions will approve major decisions. A dedicated product and delivery team will manage the platform, integrations, user experience, adoption, measurement, and support. Business-unit champions will provide feedback, identify high-value use cases, and encourage responsible adoption.

## Implementation Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to run for approximately twelve months from approval to broad deployment, followed by continuous optimization.

During months one and two, the organization will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, define governance and decision rights, assess current technology and information environments, identify priority use cases, evaluate platform options, and complete an initial legal, privacy, security, and risk assessment. The team will also define baseline measures for productivity, employee experience, support volume, and information retrieval.

During months three and four, the program will configure the selected platform and prepare the pilot. Work will include identity integration, access-control design, data-source assessment, connector configuration, security testing, logging, monitoring, content curation, policy development, and creation of training and communications materials. A representative pilot group of approximately 300 to 500 employees will be selected from functions with varied work patterns and risk profiles.

During months five and six, the pilot will operate under controlled conditions. Participants will receive training on effective prompting, source verification, confidential information, human review, and acceptable use. The project team will monitor usage, response quality, security events, user feedback, and business outcomes. Pilot use cases will be evaluated against predefined criteria, and the platform, policies, and training will be adjusted based on findings.

During months seven and eight, the organization will prepare for scale. High-value use cases from the pilot will be refined, additional integrations will be implemented, support processes will be expanded, and business-unit champions will be trained. The organization will publish practical guidance, frequently asked questions, examples, and escalation procedures. A second deployment wave of approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees will validate the operating model at greater scale.

During months nine through twelve, the assistant will be rolled out in successive waves to the remaining workforce. Each wave will include communications, training, access provisioning, usage monitoring, and a post-deployment review. High-risk or technically complex functions may receive tailored controls or delayed access. At the end of this phase, the organization will conduct a formal benefits and risk review and approve the roadmap for the following year.

After the initial twelve-month implementation, the assistant will enter a continuous-improvement operating cycle. This cycle will include model and platform updates, knowledge-source maintenance, quarterly governance reviews, use-case expansion, performance testing, employee feedback, and periodic reassessment of legal, privacy, security, and operational risks.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a cross-functional team with sufficient capacity to manage technology delivery, governance, adoption, and ongoing operations. During implementation, the core team should include a program director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning specialist, data and integration engineers, security architect, privacy and legal representatives, risk and compliance support, user-experience or service-design expertise, change-management and communications leads, training specialists, business analysts, and service-desk representatives.

A reasonable initial staffing model is approximately 20 to 30 full-time equivalent internal and contracted resources, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts from participating business units. The team may include eight to twelve technology and data specialists, four to six governance, security, privacy, and risk specialists, four to six adoption, communications, and training specialists, and several program, product, support, and business-analysis roles. Staffing should be adjusted based on the number of integrations, complexity of data environments, regulatory obligations, and selected platform.

The budget will include platform licensing, model or usage charges, implementation and integration services, security and privacy assessments, data preparation, training and communications, support capacity, monitoring and evaluation, and contingency funding. A provisional first-year budget range should be established during vendor selection and business-case development. The final budget should distinguish one-time implementation costs from recurring licensing, support, integration, and governance costs.

The project will also require participation from information owners and business-unit representatives. These individuals will help identify priority use cases, validate responses, review source content, define success measures, and support local adoption. Their contribution should be planned explicitly rather than treated as informal or unallocated work.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

Responsible deployment is a core requirement of the project. The organization will publish an acceptable-use standard that explains permitted and prohibited activities, employee responsibilities, data-handling expectations, verification requirements, and escalation channels. The standard will make clear that AI-generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete, biased, or outdated and that employees remain accountable for decisions and deliverables.

Security controls will include single sign-on, multifactor authentication where required, least-privilege access, encryption, environment separation, administrative role controls, audit logging, anomaly monitoring, and incident-response procedures. The platform and integrations will be tested for prompt injection, unauthorized retrieval, data leakage, malicious content, insecure connectors, and inappropriate model behavior.

Privacy and records-management requirements will be incorporated into the solution design. The organization will define what prompts and outputs are retained, for how long, under what circumstances they may be reviewed, and how they are handled under applicable policies and law. Sensitive information will be subject to additional controls, and the assistant will not be used to make decisions about individuals unless a separately approved process establishes appropriate safeguards, explainability, review, and appeal mechanisms.

The organization will maintain a catalog of approved use cases and a risk classification for each. Low-risk uses, such as drafting or summarizing non-sensitive material, may be broadly available. Medium-risk uses may require additional training, approved templates, or human review. High-risk uses will require formal assessment, documented controls, and executive or specialist approval before deployment.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the intended employee population, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value without creating unacceptable risk.

Adoption will be measured by activation, monthly active use, repeat use, use-case diversity, and participation across business units. A reasonable initial target is activation by at least 70 percent of employees within six months of broad availability and regular use by at least 40 percent, with adoption patterns monitored to ensure that usage is not concentrated only in technology-oriented teams.

Productivity and employee-experience outcomes will be measured through baseline and follow-up surveys, task-based studies, workflow metrics, and selected business-unit measures. The program should target a measurable reduction in time spent on common activities such as information retrieval, document drafting, summarization, and routine analysis. Pilot participants should report improved access to information and a meaningful improvement in their ability to complete selected tasks.

Quality and trust will be assessed through response evaluations, citation and source-verification rates, user feedback, incident reviews, and human-assessment samples. The organization should establish minimum quality thresholds for priority use cases and track hallucination, outdated-source, and inappropriate-response rates. Employee trust should improve over time, supported by clear limitations, visible source links, transparent policies, and effective support.

Risk and operational performance will be measured through security incidents, privacy events, unauthorized-access attempts, policy violations, service availability, response latency, support requests, and time to resolve defects or incidents. The target is zero material data breaches attributable to the assistant, prompt investigation of all reported issues, and service performance consistent with enterprise application standards.

The program should also demonstrate operational sustainability. Success requires an established product owner, documented governance processes, trained support staff, maintained knowledge sources, repeatable onboarding, and an approved budget for ongoing licensing and improvement.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to organizational knowledge, and establish a responsible foundation for broader AI adoption. The recommended approach balances speed with control by beginning with a representative pilot, validating value and risk management, and expanding through measured deployment waves.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the organization to begin detailed planning, platform evaluation, governance design, and pilot preparation. With strong executive sponsorship, cross-functional ownership, disciplined information management, and sustained investment in training and oversight, the organization can deliver an AI assistant that is secure, practical, widely adopted, and aligned with business and employee needs.

The assistant will be designed to complement—not replace—employee judgment and organizational expertise. The project does not include unrestricted access to all enterprise data, autonomous decision-making on behalf of the organization, unsupervised external communications, automated employment or disciplinary decisions, or the removal of existing records-management, security, legal, compliance, and approval requirements. The project team will measure performance, identify gaps in source content, refine user experience, and confirm that the assistant operates within approved controls.

Users will be informed that AI-generated content may contain errors and must be reviewed before use, particularly when it affects customers, employees, finances, legal obligations, safety, or external commitments. A clear feedback and incident-reporting process will support rapid correction and continuous improvement.

Knowledge owners will be responsible for reviewing connected content, resolving conflicting guidance, and ensuring that outdated material is removed or clearly marked. The governance group will conduct periodic reviews of usage patterns, accuracy, security events, bias risks, user feedback, and emerging regulatory requirements.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the full employee population through approved channels, operates within validated security and privacy controls, and achieves sustained employee adoption for priority use cases.

Target outcomes will include participation by at least 60 percent of employees within the first six months after enterprise launch, with at least 35 percent using the assistant monthly. For priority use cases, the organization should achieve a measurable reduction in the time required to locate information or complete routine drafting and summarization tasks, with an initial target of 20 percent or more compared with the baseline established before the pilot.

At least 80 percent of pilot and early-launch users should report that the assistant improves their ability to complete selected tasks. Responses to questions involving approved internal knowledge should meet an agreed accuracy and source-grounding threshold, such as 90 percent or higher for validated priority scenarios. The organization should also demonstrate a reduction in repetitive information requests to designated support teams where the assistant is intended to provide first-line guidance.

Security and trust measures are equally important. The deployment should have no unresolved critical security or privacy findings at launch, documented remediation for all high-severity findings, successful completion of access-control testing, and established procedures for monitoring and responding to incidents. All connected knowledge domains should have accountable owners and documented review cycles.

The program will use a balanced scorecard covering adoption, productivity, answer quality, user satisfaction, support impact, content health, accessibility, security, privacy, and responsible-use indicators. Results will be reviewed monthly during rollout and quarterly thereafter. Expansion into additional integrations or higher-risk use cases will occur only when performance, governance, and user trust meet agreed thresholds.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization presents a significant opportunity to improve access to knowledge, reduce routine administrative effort, and strengthen employee productivity. Success will depend not only on selecting capable technology, but also on preparing high-quality information, respecting existing permissions, establishing clear accountability, training employees, and measuring outcomes rigorously.

A phased, governed deployment will allow the organization to realize early value while controlling risk and learning from real-world use. With executive sponsorship, cross-functional ownership, disciplined implementation, and continuous oversight, the internal AI assistant can become a trusted enterprise capability that supports employees and scales with the organization’s evolving needs.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

Our organization is evaluating the deployment of an internal AI assistant to help employees find information, complete routine tasks, analyze documents, and work more efficiently. With approximately 5,000 employees across multiple functions and locations, employees often spend significant time searching for policies, locating relevant documents, drafting communications, summarizing information, and navigating internal systems. These activities create avoidable delays, duplicate effort, and inconsistent access to organizational knowledge.

An enterprise AI assistant can provide a secure, governed interface for accessing approved internal knowledge and supporting common workplace activities. By integrating with existing collaboration, document-management, and business systems, the assistant can help employees obtain faster answers while preserving appropriate permissions, privacy, and regulatory controls.

The proposed initiative will establish a scalable internal AI capability, beginning with carefully selected use cases and expanding through measured adoption. The program will combine technology deployment, data governance, security controls, user training, and change management to ensure that the assistant is useful, trusted, and aligned with organizational priorities.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to deploy a secure and reliable AI assistant that improves employee productivity while maintaining appropriate controls over organizational information.

The project will pursue the following outcomes:

- Provide employees with a single, intuitive interface for asking questions, summarizing documents, drafting content, and completing approved workflows.
- Improve the speed and consistency of access to internal policies, procedures, institutional knowledge, and business information.
- Reduce time spent on repetitive administrative and information-retrieval tasks.
- Support employees without replacing accountability, professional judgment, or established approval processes.
- Establish enterprise standards for AI security, privacy, governance, responsible use, and performance monitoring.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled applications and business-process automation.
- Demonstrate measurable value through productivity, adoption, satisfaction, and operational-efficiency metrics.

## Scope

The project will include the design, configuration, deployment, and operationalization of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The initial solution will be accessible through approved enterprise channels, such as the organization’s collaboration platform, intranet, or employee portal.

The assistant’s initial capabilities will include natural-language question answering over approved internal content; document summarization and comparison; drafting and editing of common business communications; meeting and information synthesis; assistance with policies, procedures, and frequently asked questions; and guided support for selected internal processes. Where appropriate, the assistant will provide links to source materials and identify when information is incomplete, uncertain, or subject to human review.

The project will include integration with selected repositories and systems, such as the document-management platform, knowledge base, intranet, collaboration tools, and approved enterprise applications. Integrations will be prioritized according to business value, data quality, technical feasibility, and security risk. Access to content will respect existing identity, role-based permissions, and information-classification requirements.

Governance and risk controls are included in scope. These will cover identity and access management, data-loss prevention, privacy and retention, audit logging, model and prompt monitoring, acceptable-use policies, human oversight, incident response, vendor management, and procedures for reporting inaccurate or harmful outputs.

The initial deployment will focus on general employee productivity and knowledge-access use cases. High-risk or highly regulated applications—such as automated employment decisions, legal determinations, clinical or safety decisions, financial approvals, or autonomous execution of consequential transactions—will not be included in the initial release unless separately assessed and approved through the organization’s governance process.

The project will also include employee communications, training, support processes, adoption measurement, and a structured feedback program. Custom model development is not expected in the first phase; the implementation will use an enterprise-grade managed AI service or platform selected through the organization’s procurement, security, and architecture processes.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to run for approximately nine months from approval to enterprise launch, followed by an ongoing optimization phase.

During **Months 1 and 2**, the project team will establish governance, confirm executive sponsorship, define priority use cases, assess the organization’s data environment, and complete the technology and vendor evaluation. This phase will produce the target architecture, risk assessment, implementation plan, baseline productivity measures, and initial policy framework. Business units will be engaged to identify pilot participants and representative workflows.

During **Months 3 and 4**, the team will configure the assistant, establish identity and access controls, connect initial knowledge sources, and implement monitoring and security controls. Content will be assessed for accuracy, ownership, duplication, sensitivity, and lifecycle status. The team will also develop prompt guidance, employee-facing usage standards, support procedures, and training materials.

During **Months 5 and 6**, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 250 to 500 employees across a representative set of functions, locations, and technical environments. Pilot participants will receive training and structured guidance. The project team will measure response quality, usability, adoption, productivity impact, security events, and support demand. Feedback will be used to improve content connections, user experience, policies, and operational controls.

During **Months 7 and 8**, the solution will be expanded to a broader early-adopter group of approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees. Additional approved knowledge sources and use cases will be introduced in stages. The team will validate readiness for scale, refine training and communications, address identified risks, and confirm that service-level, support, and monitoring arrangements are adequate for organization-wide use.

During **Month 9**, the assistant will be launched to the full employee population through a phased rollout. Communications will explain the assistant’s capabilities, limitations, approved uses, and escalation channels. Rollout sequencing may be adjusted by business unit to manage support demand and ensure that high-priority groups receive appropriate preparation.

Following launch, the organization will enter an ongoing optimization phase. Performance, adoption, user feedback, knowledge quality, and risk indicators will be reviewed regularly. New integrations and higher-value use cases will be introduced only after appropriate technical, security, legal, privacy, and business review.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require executive sponsorship and cross-functional participation from technology, security, privacy, legal, procurement, records management, human resources, communications, learning and development, and representative business units.

A core delivery team is expected to include a program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning specialist, data and knowledge engineer, security architect, privacy or compliance lead, legal advisor, user-experience designer, change-management lead, training specialist, communications lead, and service-management representative. Business-unit subject-matter experts will be needed to validate use cases, assess source content, test responses, and support adoption.

The organization should plan for approximately 10 to 15 dedicated full-time-equivalent roles during the implementation period, supplemented by part-time contributions from business, legal, security, data-governance, and operational teams. After launch, a smaller permanent operating team will be required to manage the platform, monitor performance, maintain integrations, review content quality, coordinate enhancements, and administer governance.

Technology requirements will include an enterprise AI platform or managed service; secure identity and access integration; connectors to approved content repositories; logging and monitoring; data-loss-prevention capabilities; testing and evaluation tools; service-management integration; and appropriate development, test, and production environments. The selected platform must support enterprise data protections, contractual restrictions on data use, administrative controls, auditability, availability targets, and integration with existing architecture.

The budget will include platform licensing or consumption costs, implementation services, integration development, security and privacy assessment, data remediation, user research, training, communications, support, and ongoing operations. A contingency should be reserved for unexpected data-quality issues, additional security requirements, licensing changes, and integration complexity. Final cost estimates should be developed after vendor selection and completion of the technical discovery phase.

## Governance and Risk Management

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define acceptable and prohibited uses, accountability for outputs, data-handling requirements, human-review expectations, model evaluation standards, records-management obligations, and procedures for escalating incidents or inaccurate responses.

The assistant will not be presented as an infallible source of truth. Responses should identify supporting sources where available and encourage users to verify information when decisions are material, sensitive, or consequential. Employees will remain responsible for reviewing generated content and complying with applicable policies and professional requirements.

Access controls will be enforced through the organization’s existing identity and authorization systems. The assistant will not grant users access to information they could not otherwise access. Sensitive information will be subject to classification, retention, masking, and monitoring requirements. Prompts, responses, and usage data will be handled according to approved privacy and records-management standards.

Before each major release, the team will conduct testing for accuracy, relevance, harmful or biased outputs, prompt injection, unauthorized disclosure, data leakage, resilience, and performance. Significant defects or security issues will trigger documented remediation and, where necessary, suspension of affected capabilities.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the full employee population, operates within approved security and governance controls, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

Target success measures will include:

- At least 60 percent of employees actively using the assistant within six months of full deployment.
- At least 40 percent of eligible employees using the assistant monthly on a sustained basis.
- A measurable reduction in time spent locating information and completing selected routine tasks, with an initial target of 20 percent in prioritized use cases.
- User satisfaction of at least  zadovolj? 
- At least 75 percent of surveyed users reporting that the assistant improves their ability to complete applicable tasks.
- Response-quality ratings of at least 85 percent for approved pilot and production use cases, based on a defined evaluation set and user feedback.
- No material unauthorized disclosure of confidential or restricted information.
- Completion of required privacy, security, legal, and governance reviews before each deployment stage.
- Defined support service levels, documented incident procedures, and successful handoff to a permanent operating team.
- A validated business case for continued investment, including documented productivity benefits, adoption patterns, operational costs, and prioritized opportunities for expansion.

In addition to quantitative measures, the organization will evaluate whether employees trust the assistant, understand its limitations, and use it responsibly. Success will therefore be measured not only by usage volume, but also by the quality of outcomes, reduction in friction, responsible behavior, and sustained business value.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents an opportunity to improve access to knowledge, reduce repetitive work, and establish a practical foundation for responsible enterprise AI. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while learning from real-world usage and managing technical, operational, and reputational risk.

With executive sponsorship, strong governance, high-quality knowledge sources, disciplined implementation, and sustained change management, the organization can introduce an AI assistant that is secure, useful, and scalable. Approval of this proposal will authorize the discovery and implementation program, beginning with governance and priority-use-case definition and progressing through pilot, measured expansion, and organization-wide deployment.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Organizations are increasingly using artificial intelligence to improve productivity, accelerate access to information, and support better decision-making. Within our 5,000-employee organization, employees currently spend significant time searching for policies, procedures, project documentation, and institutional knowledge across disconnected systems. Common tasks such as drafting communications, summarizing documents, analyzing information, preparing reports, and answering routine operational questions are often performed manually and inconsistently.

An internal AI assistant would provide employees with a secure, centrally managed interface for accessing approved organizational knowledge and receiving support with common work activities. The assistant would be designed for enterprise use, with appropriate identity controls, data protections, auditability, and governance. It would complement—not replace—employee judgment, established approval processes, or specialized business systems.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment beginning with a controlled pilot and expanding to the broader organization after validation. The approach is intended to deliver measurable value while managing risks related to privacy, security, accuracy, intellectual property, regulatory obligations, and inappropriate use.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to deploy a trusted internal AI assistant that improves employee productivity and access to organizational knowledge while maintaining strong governance and security controls.

The assistant will enable employees to locate and summarize approved internal information, draft and refine business content, generate meeting and document summaries, support research and analysis, and receive guidance on standard processes. Where appropriate, it will connect to selected enterprise repositories and applications so that responses can be grounded in current, authorized information.

The project will also establish a repeatable operating model for enterprise AI, including acceptable-use standards, data classification requirements, human-review expectations, model evaluation procedures, incident response processes, and ongoing performance monitoring. The deployment will prioritize practical business value, adoption, transparency, and responsible use.

## Scope

The initial scope includes the selection and configuration of an enterprise AI assistant platform; integration with the organization’s identity and access-management systems; connection to a defined set of approved knowledge sources; establishment of security, privacy, governance, and support processes; and deployment to employees through approved digital channels.

The first release will focus on broadly applicable use cases, including document drafting and editing, summarization, enterprise knowledge search, meeting preparation and follow-up, communication support, and assistance with routine administrative tasks. Business units may propose additional use cases, but those involving highly sensitive data, automated decisions affecting individuals, external customer commitments, regulated activities, or direct execution of transactions will require separate review and approval.

The project will include a pilot group representing corporate functions, operational teams, technical users, managers, and a range of employee roles. Pilot participants will receive training and will provide structured feedback on usefulness, accuracy, usability, and risk. The pilot will be followed by a staged organizational rollout based on defined readiness criteria.

The initial scope does not include fully autonomous decision-making, unsupervised external communications, replacement of line-of-business applications, or unrestricted access to all organizational data. The assistant will not be treated as an authoritative source where policies, legal requirements, financial controls, or professional judgment apply. Employees will remain responsible for verifying outputs and complying with existing procedures.

## Approach and Governance

The project will be sponsored by the executive leadership team and governed by a cross-functional steering committee consisting of representatives from information technology, information security, legal, privacy, compliance, human resources, records management, communications, procurement, and key business units.

A product owner will be responsible for the assistant’s roadmap, prioritization, user experience, and adoption. Technical leads will oversee platform configuration, integrations, identity management, data architecture, monitoring, and operational support. Legal, privacy, security, and compliance specialists will review use cases, contractual terms, data handling, access controls, and risk mitigations.

The assistant will use role-based access controls and existing employee identity systems wherever possible. Connected repositories will be onboarded only after confirming ownership, data quality, permissions, retention requirements, and appropriate indexing methods. Sensitive information will be handled according to existing data-classification policies. Logging and monitoring will be implemented to support troubleshooting, security investigations, usage analysis, and continuous improvement, subject to applicable privacy and employment requirements.

A responsible-use framework will be published before broad deployment. It will explain permitted and prohibited uses, limitations of AI-generated content, verification responsibilities, handling of confidential information, requirements for human approval, and procedures for reporting inaccurate, harmful, or inappropriate responses. Training will be mandatory for initial users and incorporated into broader employee enablement activities as the service expands.

## Timeline

The project is expected to take approximately nine months from initiation through organization-wide availability.

During the first month, the project team will confirm executive sponsorship, establish governance, define target use cases, assess existing platforms, document requirements, and complete an initial risk and data-readiness assessment.

During months two and three, the team will select or confirm the technology platform, negotiate required vendor terms, configure identity and security controls, define the service architecture, prepare initial knowledge sources, and develop governance, support, and training materials. The team will also establish baseline measures for productivity, search effectiveness, user satisfaction, and support demand.

During months four and five, the assistant will be developed and tested in a controlled environment. Testing will include functional performance, access control, data leakage prevention, prompt and response quality, resilience, accessibility, usability, and adversarial or misuse scenarios. Selected employees will participate in user acceptance testing, and identified issues will be addressed before pilot launch.

During month six, the organization will conduct a pilot involving approximately 250 to 400 employees. Pilot users will receive training, access support channels, and complete structured feedback activities. Usage patterns, response quality, security events, and business outcomes will be monitored closely.

During month seven, the project team will evaluate pilot results and make a formal go/no-go recommendation for broader deployment. The decision will be based on security and privacy readiness, service reliability, user adoption, demonstrated business value, manageable support requirements, and evidence that known risks are adequately controlled.

During months eight and nine, the assistant will be rolled out in waves to the broader workforce. Each wave will include communications, training, local business-unit support, and post-launch monitoring. Following the initial rollout, the service will transition to a steady-state operating model with quarterly reviews of performance, risk, usage, and the prioritized enhancement backlog.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a dedicated cross-functional team throughout implementation. Core staffing should include a project or program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or platform engineer, data and integration engineers, information-security representative, privacy and legal advisors, user-experience or service-design support, change-management and communications leads, training specialists, business analysts, and service-desk representatives.

The expected implementation effort is approximately 10 to 14 full-time equivalent positions distributed across the project period, supplemented by part-time participation from subject-matter experts and representatives of business units. After deployment, the organization should maintain a smaller permanent team responsible for product management, platform administration, knowledge-source management, model and response evaluation, security monitoring, user support, training, and governance.

The technology budget will include platform licensing or usage charges, enterprise integration, identity and access management, security monitoring, storage and data processing, testing tools, support services, and potential vendor implementation assistance. Additional funding may be required to improve the quality and structure of source content before it is connected to the assistant. A contingency should be reserved for unexpected integration work, compliance requirements, performance improvements, and adoption activities.

Business-unit leaders will need to allocate employee time for use-case definition, content validation, pilot participation, training, and feedback. Information owners will remain responsible for ensuring that connected content is accurate, current, appropriately classified, and available to the correct audiences.

## Risks and Mitigations

The most significant risks include inaccurate or misleading responses, unauthorized disclosure of information, inappropriate reliance on AI-generated content, inconsistent source data, low employee adoption, unanticipated operating costs, and unclear accountability for AI-supported work.

These risks will be managed through controlled data access, source attribution where available, clear user guidance, mandatory human review for consequential outputs, testing against representative scenarios, monitoring for anomalous activity, documented escalation procedures, and ongoing evaluation by business and technical experts. The project will begin with low- and moderate-risk use cases and will expand only after the organization demonstrates that controls are effective.

The assistant will be positioned as a support tool rather than an autonomous authority. Employees will be instructed to verify important outputs against authoritative sources and to follow existing approval, legal, financial, safety, and records-management processes. High-impact or regulated use cases will be subject to additional review before implementation.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the intended employee population with appropriate security, privacy, governance, accessibility, and support controls in place; when connected knowledge sources are permission-aware, reliable, and maintained by accountable owners; and when employees understand how to use the service responsibly.

Within the first six months after broad deployment, success should be demonstrated through measurable adoption and business outcomes. Target measures include participation by at least 60 percent of employees, regular monthly use by at least 40 percent of employees, and positive user satisfaction from at least 75 percent of surveyed users. The organization should also demonstrate measurable reductions in time spent locating information and completing selected high-volume tasks, with a target of at least 20 percent improvement for prioritized use cases.

Additional success measures will include response quality evaluated against agreed test sets, low rates of materially harmful or misleading outputs, no unresolved critical security or privacy incidents, high completion rates for required training, acceptable service availability, and support demand that can be handled within established service levels. Business units will be expected to document at least five validated use cases that produce measurable productivity, quality, or employee-experience benefits.

Success will not be measured by usage alone. The organization will conduct formal reviews at three, six, and twelve months after launch to assess realized value, risk performance, employee feedback, operating cost, and the need for changes to the platform or governance model.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents an opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish a responsible foundation for broader AI adoption. A phased implementation will allow the organization to learn from real use, validate controls, and focus investment on the highest-value applications.

With executive sponsorship, cross-functional governance, disciplined data and security practices, effective training, and clear accountability, the organization can introduce an AI assistant that is useful, trusted, and sustainable. Approval of this proposal will authorize the project team to begin detailed planning, platform evaluation, risk assessment, and preparation for the controlled pilot.
